sentences.text: By the middle of October he had seen it thirty-one times and he had started counting because the counting made it feel like a project rather than a problem.
It was in the car park.
It was on the wall outside the shop.
It was on the road out to the caravan site at seven in the morning, and again at four, and once at both ends of the same day.
It was in his own garden.
That was on the eighteenth, and it was the one that stopped him sleeping.
He got up for water at about one and looked out of the landing window because he always looked out of the landing window, and it was on the grass by the shed, sitting, facing the house.
It never came closer than about ten metres and it never went further than about thirty.
It never ran.
Twice he walked directly at it, in daylight, in a temper, and it stood up and moved off at a walk and stopped again when he stopped.
He tried, twice, to get somebody else to see it.

The first time was on the road by the caravan site with his mother in the car, and he said *there's a fox* in the most ordinary voice he could manage, and she said *oh yes* — and he spent the rest of the journey working out from what she said next that she had been agreeing with him rather than looking.
The second time was worse.
It was on the school wall at lunch and he said it to Effie, and pointed, and she looked exactly where he was pointing for a good four seconds and said, "Where?" He said he'd been mistaken.
She was decent about it, which he minded.
He went into the wood in the end, in the last week of October, on a Saturday, on purpose, because he had worked out what was bothering him and could not make it stop bothering him any other way.
The rule was that you saw the fox when you were lost.
He was not lost.
That was the point.
He was not lost in Fernaig wood or anywhere else; he was in a car park, and a shop doorway, and his own garden, four metres from a back door he could have found blindfolded.

So either the rule was wrong, or Effie was wrong, or — He went in at the top gate and walked for two hours, deliberately, badly, taking every wrong turn he could identify, and got himself thoroughly and genuinely lost somewhere in the middle by about half two.
He stood there in the wet bracken, properly disoriented, no idea which way the road was.
And there was no fox.

He came out an hour later at the quarry side, scratched and extremely cold, having established the one thing he had least wanted to establish, which was that the rule worked fine and that the problem was him.
He sat on the wall at the quarry for a while before going home, working it through.
If the rule was about woods, he was fine and the fox was a coincidence and foxes are common.

If the rule was not about woods, then something in Fernaig had decided he was lost — had been deciding it, daily, since the twelfth of September, in car parks and shop doorways and his own back garden — and had gone to the trouble of sitting down in his eyeline about thirty-one times to say so.
And the second one was ridiculous, and he believed it, and he could not think of a single person in that village he could say it to.
